title: Payment Gateway: Complete Architecture
description: Design a high-security payment processing platform (Stripe scale) with PCI-DSS card tokenization, idempotent transactions, and double-entry ledgering.

data.text: Design a secure, global payment gateway and financial processing platform similar to Stripe or Adyen. The system processes credit cards, digital wallets (Apple Pay, Google Pay), and direct bank rails across hundreds of thousands of merchants. The core engineering challenges involve strict zero-tolerance financial data integrity: maintaining PCI-DSS Level 1 compliance through isolated card tokenization, guaranteeing zero duplicate charges via idempotent execution, running real-time fraud screening, orchestrating two-phase authorization/capture with acquiring banks, and maintaining an immutable double-entry ledger for daily reconciliation.

terms.definition: An isolated, air-gapped security zone storing raw Primary Account Numbers (PAN) and CVVs, returning non-sensitive surrogate tokens (`tok_xxx`) to merchant servers.
Authorization places a temporary hold on the cardholder's credit line; Capture finalizes the transfer of funds when goods ship.
Using a client-supplied `Idempotency-Key` to cache in-flight and completed transaction states, ensuring network retries return identical responses without re-executing charges.
An immutable accounting paradigm where every transaction records equal and offsetting Debit and Credit entries across accounts, ensuring sum(balance) == 0.
The Acquiring Bank processes transactions on behalf of the merchant; the Issuing Bank holds the customer's credit/debit account.

data.title: Functional Requirements
items: Card Tokenization: Client-side SDK (Stripe Elements) tokenizes raw card details directly to a PCI vault
Payment Processing: Authorize, Capture, Void, and Refund credit card, debit card, and wallet transactions
Idempotent APIs: Safeguard against duplicate charges from browser double-clicks or network retry storms
Real-Time Fraud Detection: Score risk using transaction velocity, geolocation, IP reputation, and 3D Secure (3DS)
Double-Entry Ledger: Maintain an immutable ledger recording all merchant balances, payouts, and fees
Merchant Webhooks: Reliably notify merchant backend systems of asynchronous payment status events with HMAC signatures

data.title: Non-Functional Requirements
items: Data Integrity: Exactly-once financial semantics; zero duplicate charges or phantom ledger balances
Security Compliance: Strict PCI-DSS Level 1 compliance; raw card numbers never touch general application logs or databases
Authorization Latency: Sub-1.5s P99 latency end-to-end (including acquiring bank and card network hops)
Scale: 10,000+ payment transactions/sec; millions of daily merchant webhook deliveries
Availability: 99.999% uptime for the payment authorization API

data.text: To maintain strict PCI-DSS scope reduction, raw card credentials never hit merchant servers or internal application microservices. Browser clients communicate directly with an isolated Tokenization Vault, while downstream services process tokenized payments through an idempotent SAGA orchestrator.

faqs.question: How is PCI-DSS Level 1 compliance achieved without massive audit overhead?
faqs.answer: By enforcing strict scope reduction. Using hosted iFrames (e.g. Stripe Elements), the merchant website never receives, processes, or transmits credit card numbers. The customer types the 16-digit card number directly into the iFrame hosted by the PCI Vault domain. The merchant server only receives a non-PCI token (`tok_123`), exempting 99% of company microservices from onerous PCI-DSS audit requirements.

faqs.question: Why is a Double-Entry Ledger required instead of a simple balance column?
faqs.answer: In a single-column architecture (`balance = balance + 50`), a bug, failed transaction, or partial database rollback can silently corrupt accounts with no audit trail. In double-entry bookkeeping, money cannot be created or destroyed: every credit must have a corresponding debit. If total debits do not equal total credits across all accounts, the ledger transaction is rejected, providing mathematical proof of financial integrity.

faqs.question: How does Idempotency protect against network timeouts during bank authorization?
faqs.answer: If an API client sends a payment request and experiences a network timeout before receiving the response, it will retry the call. The payment gateway stores the `Idempotency-Key` in an "IN_PROGRESS" state. If a duplicate arrives while the bank is still processing, the second request waits; when completed, the cached authorization result is returned without calling the card network a second time.

faqs.question: How are Webhooks delivered reliably to merchants during downtime?
faqs.answer: Merchant webhooks are published to Kafka and consumed by a dedicated delivery worker fleet. If the merchant endpoint returns HTTP 5xx or times out, the message enters a dead-letter retry topic with exponential backoff (e.g. retry after 1m, 5m, 15m, 1h, up to 72 hours). Every webhook payload includes an HMAC-SHA256 signature header so the merchant can verify authentic gateway origin.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Client-side iFrame tokenization limits PCI-DSS scope to an isolated, secure vault tier
Strict idempotency keys with atomic Redis state locks eliminate duplicate charges from network retries
Two-phase authorization and capture decouples payment reservation from warehouse fulfillment
Immutable double-entry ledger bookkeeping ensures financial balance integrity with zero drift
Signed HMAC webhooks with exponential backoff retries guarantee reliable merchant notifications
data.takeaway: Payment gateways demand zero-error fault tolerance: tokenized PCI vaults safeguard credit credentials while idempotent state machines and double-entry ledgers ensure mathematical precision for every financial transaction.
